blocks.prompt: The Little Red Hunter
blocks.text: A ladybug is small, but it is a hunter. On the back of a leaf live tiny green bugs called aphids. Aphids drink the juice out of plants. Too many aphids can make a plant sick. The ladybug walks along the leaf and eats them. One ladybug can eat fifty aphids in a day. Farmers are glad to see ladybugs in the garden. Birds are not glad. To a bird, red and black means stop. It means this one will taste bad. So the bird flies past, and the ladybug keeps eating.

blocks.prompt: Wrong Name, Strange Baby
blocks.text: Here is a surprise. A ladybug is not a bug at all. It is a beetle. Scientists who study insects often call it a lady beetle instead, and in England people call it a ladybird. None of those names are wrong. They are just different. Here is a bigger surprise. A baby ladybug looks nothing like its parents. It hatches from a tiny yellow egg as a larva: long, black, spiky, and orange in places, crawling over the leaf like a very small alligator. Most people who find one have no idea what it is. Some even squash it, thinking it is a pest. It is not. The larva eats aphids all day long, hundreds of them before it is done growing. When it has eaten enough, the larva glues itself to a leaf and turns into a pupa. Inside that hard shell, its whole body is rebuilt. About a week later the shell splits and a ladybug climbs out. It is pale yellow and soft. Its spots are not there yet. Over the next few hours the shell hardens, the red comes in, and the spots appear one by one.

blocks.prompt: The Wings Under the Red Lid
blocks.text: A ladybug's red back is not a back. It is a pair of wings. They are called elytra, and they are the ladybug's front wings, hardened into curved shells. They are no good for flying. Their job is armor. They lock down over the ladybug's body like the lid of a box and keep the soft parts safe. The real flying wings are hidden underneath, and they are the strange part. They are much longer than the elytra that cover them. To fit, they fold. Each wing is creased along its veins and packs itself down like a paper fan, and when the ladybug wants to go, the elytra lift, the wings spring open in a fraction of a second, and it is airborne. Engineers have filmed this happening through a see-through fake elytron, glued on in place of the real one, just to watch how the folding works. They want to borrow the trick for things like satellite antennas that must ride to space folded and open perfectly once. The ladybug has one more trick, and it is rude. If something grabs it, it squeezes a drop of yellow liquid out of its knee joints. The liquid stinks and tastes bitter. A bird that bites one ladybug remembers, and the red and black tells it which insects to leave alone. The color is not decoration. It is a warning label.

blocks.prompt: Everything You Know About the Spots
blocks.text: Almost everything people think they know about ladybug spots is wrong. Start with the oldest story. In medieval Europe, aphids were destroying crops, and farmers had no way to fight them. They prayed to the Virgin Mary. Small red beetles arrived and ate the aphids, and the farmers gave them her name: Our Lady's beetle. In England it became ladybird. In America it became ladybug, which is unfortunate, because the animal is not a bug. True bugs are a separate group with piercing mouthparts. A ladybug is a beetle. Entomologists tend to say lady beetle and quietly correct the rest of us. Now the myth you have probably heard: that you can count a ladybug's spots to learn its age. You cannot. The spots do not change. What they tell you is the species. The seven-spotted ladybug wears seven and always has, from the hour its shell hardened. There are roughly five thousand species of lady beetle, and they come in red, orange, yellow, black, and combinations of all of them, with spots, stripes, or nothing at all. The color itself is doing real work. Biologists call it aposematism, a warning signal aimed at anything with eyes and an appetite. Red on black is loud, easy to remember, and it is not a bluff. Pinch a ladybug and it bleeds on purpose, pushing a bitter yellow fluid out through its leg joints. A young bird tries one, gags, and never repeats the mistake. Every ladybug afterward is protected by that bird's bad memory. Winter reveals another habit. As the cold comes, ladybugs stop hunting and gather. They pack into rock cracks, under bark, beneath leaf litter, sometimes in the corners of houses, thousands of bodies pressed together in one huddle. They are not hibernating exactly. They are waiting, burning stored fat, holding on for the first warm day and the first aphids of spring.

blocks.prompt: The Beetle That Saved the Orange Groves, and the One That Should Have Stayed Home
blocks.text: In 1868 a nurseryman in Menlo Park, California, imported some acacia plants from Australia. Something came with them. Icerya purchasi, the cottony cushion scale, is a small sap-sucking insect that wraps itself in a white fluted egg sac and clamps onto a branch, and it has almost no enemies outside Australia. In California it found endless citrus and nothing to stop it. Within twenty years it was killing orange and lemon trees faster than growers could replant. Southern California's citrus industry, then young and enormous in ambition, was close to finished. Orchards were being cut down and burned. Charles Riley, the chief entomologist of the United States Department of Agriculture, had an idea that sounded absurd to most people: if the pest had no enemies here, go find its enemies where it came from. Congress had blocked the department from paying for foreign travel, so Riley sent Albert Koebele to Australia in 1888 on the excuse of attending an exhibition in Melbourne. Koebele hunted through Australian orchards for whatever was eating cottony cushion scale and shipped what he found back to Daniel Coquillett in Los Angeles. Among the shipments were a few dozen small red beetles, Rodolia cardinalis, now called the vedalia beetle. Coquillett released them under a tented orange tree in a Los Angeles grove and waited. The beetles ate. They bred. The tent came off, and they spread through the county on their own. Within about two years the scale had collapsed and the orange shipments were rising again. The whole rescue cost a couple of thousand dollars. It is still the most quoted success in the history of biological control, and it created an idea that felt like a law of nature: import a predator, solve a pest. That idea has a receipt attached, and North America is still paying it. Harmonia axyridis, the harlequin lady beetle, was brought over from Asia through the twentieth century to do the same job on aphids. It did the job well. It also did everything else. It is larger and greedier than native ladybugs, and it eats them, including their eggs and larvae. The nine-spotted ladybug, once so common that New York made it the state insect, became so scarce that for years nobody could find one, and a search project eventually turned up a small population on Long Island. Harlequins swarm into houses by the thousands each fall, bite, stain walls with reflex blood, and get harvested with wine grapes, where a few of them are enough to taint an entire batch. Same family, same logic, opposite result. The vedalia beetle was a specialist that ate one thing and starved without it. The harlequin was a generalist that would eat almost anything, and a generalist you release is a generalist you cannot recall. The lesson took a century to learn, and it was expensive.
